blocks.text: RESOLUTION Recognizing the duty of the Federal Government to create a Green New Deal.
Preamble

Whereas the October 2018 report entitled "Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5 °C" by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the November 2018 Fourth National Climate Assessment report found that--
(1) human activity is the dominant cause of observed climate change over the past century;

(2) a changing climate is causing sea levels to rise and an increase in wildfires, severe storms, droughts, and other extreme weather events that threaten human life, healthy communities, and critical infrastructure;
(3) global warming at or above 2 degrees Celsius beyond preindustrialized levels will cause--
(A) mass migration from the regions most affected by climate change;
(B) more than $500,000,000,000 in lost annual economic output in the United States by the year 2100;
(C) wildfires that, by 2050, will annually burn at least twice as much forest area in the western United States than was typically burned by wildfires in the years preceding 2019;
(D) a loss of more than 99 percent of all coral reefs on Earth;
(E) more than 350,000,000 more people to be exposed globally to deadly heat stress by 2050; and
(F) a risk of damage to $1,000,000,000,000 of public infrastructure and coastal real estate in the United States; and
(4) global temperatures must be kept below 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrialized levels to avoid the most severe impacts of a changing climate, which will require--
(A) global reductions in greenhouse gas emissions from human sources of 40 to 60 percent from 2010 levels by 2030; and
(B) net-zero global emissions by 2050;

Whereas, because the United States has historically been responsible for a disproportionate amount of greenhouse gas emissions, having emitted 20 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions through 2014, and has a high technological capacity, the United States must take a leading role in reducing emissions through economic transformation;
Whereas the United States is currently experiencing several related crises, with--

(1) life expectancy declining while basic needs, such as clean air, clean water, healthy food, and adequate health care, housing, transportation, and education, are inaccessible to a significant portion of the United States population;
(2) a 4-decade trend of wage stagnation, deindustrialization, and antilabor policies that has led to--
(A) hourly wages overall stagnating since the 1970s despite increased worker productivity;
(B) the third-worst level of socioeconomic mobility in the developed world before the Great Recession;
(C) the erosion of the earning and bargaining power of workers in the United States; and
(D) inadequate resources for public sector workers to confront the challenges of climate change at local, State, and Federal levels; and
(3) the greatest income inequality since the 1920s, with--
(A) the top 1 percent of earners accruing 91 percent of gains in the first few years of economic recovery after the Great Recession;
(B) a large racial wealth divide amounting to a difference of 20 times more wealth between the average white family and the average black family; and
(C) a gender earnings gap that results in women earning approximately 80 percent as much as men, at the median;

Whereas climate change, pollution, and environmental destruction have exacerbated systemic racial, regional, social, environmental, and economic injustices (referred to in this preamble as "systemic injustices") by disproportionately affecting indigenous peoples, communities of color, migrant communities, deindustrialized communities, depopulated rural communities, the poor, low-income workers, women, the elderly, the unhoused, people with disabilities, and youth (referred to in this preamble as "frontline and vulnerable communities");
Whereas, climate change constitutes a direct threat to the national security of the United States--
(1) by impacting the economic, environmental, and social stability of countries and communities around the world; and
(2) by acting as a threat multiplier;

Whereas the Federal Government-led mobilizations during World War II and the New Deal created the greatest middle class that the United States has ever seen, but many members of frontline and vulnerable communities were excluded from many of the economic and societal benefits of those mobilizations; and

Whereas the House of Representatives recognizes that a new national, social, industrial, and economic mobilization on a scale not seen since World War II and the New Deal era is a historic opportunity--
(1) to create millions of good, high-wage jobs in the United States;
(2) to provide unprecedented levels of prosperity and economic security for all people of the United States; and
(3) to counteract systemic injustices: Now, therefore, be it
Resolving clause
Resolved, That it is the sense of the House of Representatives that--
(1) it is the duty of the Federal Government to create a Green New Deal--
(A) to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions through a fair and just transition for all communities and workers;
(B) to create millions of good, high-wage jobs and ensure prosperity and economic security for all people of the United States;
(C) to invest in the infrastructure and industry of the United States to sustainably meet the challenges of the 21st century;
(D) to secure for all people of the United States for generations to come--
(i) clean air and water;
(ii) climate and community resiliency;
(iii) healthy food;
(iv) access to nature; and
(v) a sustainable environment; and

(E) to promote justice and equity by stopping current, preventing future, and repairing historic oppression of indigenous peoples, communities of color, migrant communities, deindustrialized communities, depopulated rural communities, the poor, low-income workers, women, the elderly, the unhoused, people with disabilities, and youth (referred to in this resolution as "frontline and vulnerable communities");

(2) the goals described in subparagraphs (A) through (E) of paragraph (1) (referred to in this resolution as the "Green New Deal goals") should be accomplished through a 10-year national mobilization (referred to in this resolution as the "Green New Deal mobilization") that will require the following goals and projects--
(A) building resiliency against climate change-related disasters, such as extreme weather, including by leveraging funding and providing investments for community-defined projects and strategies;
(B) repairing and upgrading the infrastructure in the United States, including--
(i) by eliminating pollution and greenhouse gas emissions as much as technologically feasible;
(ii) by guaranteeing universal access to clean water;
(iii) by reducing the risks posed by climate impacts; and
(iv) by ensuring that any infrastructure bill considered by Congress addresses climate change;
(C) meeting 100 percent of the power demand in the United States through clean, renewable, and zero-emission energy sources, including--
(i) by dramatically expanding and upgrading renewable power sources; and
(ii) by deploying new capacity;
(D) building or upgrading to energy-efficient, distributed, and "smart" power grids, and ensuring affordable access to electricity;

(E) upgrading all existing buildings in the United States and building new buildings to achieve maximum energy efficiency, water efficiency, safety, affordability, comfort, and durability, including through electrification;

(F) spurring massive growth in clean manufacturing in the United States and removing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing and industry as much as is technologically feasible, including by expanding renewable energy manufacturing and investing in existing manufacturing and industry;

(G) working collaboratively with farmers and ranchers in the United States to remove pollution and greenhouse gas emissions from the agricultural sector as much as is technologically feasible, including--
(i) by supporting family farming;
(ii) by investing in sustainable farming and land use practices that increase soil health; and
(iii) by building a more sustainable food system that ensures universal access to healthy food;

(H) overhauling transportation systems in the United States to remove pollution and greenhouse gas emissions from the transportation sector as much as is technologically feasible, including through investment in--
(i) zero-emission vehicle infrastructure and manufacturing;
(ii) clean, affordable, and accessible public transit; and
(iii) high-speed rail;
(I) mitigating and managing the long-term adverse health, economic, and other effects of pollution and climate change, including by providing funding for community-defined projects and strategies;

(J) removing greenhouse gases from the atmosphere and reducing pollution by restoring natural ecosystems through proven low-tech solutions that increase soil carbon storage, such as land preservation and afforestation;
(K) restoring and protecting threatened, endangered, and fragile ecosystems through locally appropriate and science-based projects that enhance biodiversity and support climate resiliency;
(L) cleaning up existing hazardous waste and abandoned sites, ensuring economic development and sustainability on those sites;
(M) identifying other emission and pollution sources and creating solutions to remove them; and

(N) promoting the international exchange of technology, expertise, products, funding, and services, with the aim of making the United States the international leader on climate action, and to help other countries achieve a Green New Deal;

(3) a Green New Deal must be developed through transparent and inclusive consultation, collaboration, and partnership with frontline and vulnerable communities, labor unions, worker cooperatives, civil society groups, academia, and businesses; and
(4) to achieve the Green New Deal goals and mobilization, a Green New Deal will require the following goals and projects--

(A) providing and leveraging, in a way that ensures that the public receives appropriate ownership stakes and returns on investment, adequate capital (including through community grants, public banks, and other public financing), technical expertise, supporting policies, and other forms of assistance to communities, organizations, Federal, State, and local government agencies, and businesses working on the Green New Deal mobilization;
(B) ensuring that the Federal Government takes into account the complete environmental and social costs and impacts of emissions through--
(i) existing laws;
(ii) new policies and programs; and
(iii) ensuring that frontline and vulnerable communities shall not be adversely affected;

(C) providing resources, training, and high-quality education, including higher education, to all people of the United States, with a focus on frontline and vulnerable communities, so that all people of the United States may be full and equal participants in the Green New Deal mobilization;
(D) making public investments in the research and development of new clean and renewable energy technologies and industries;

(E) directing investments to spur economic development, deepen and diversify industry and business in local and regional economies, and build wealth and community ownership, while prioritizing high-quality job creation and economic, social, and environmental benefits in frontline and vulnerable communities, and deindustrialized communities, that may otherwise struggle with the transition away from greenhouse gas intensive industries;

(F) ensuring the use of democratic and participatory processes that are inclusive of and led by frontline and vulnerable communities and workers to plan, implement, and administer the Green New Deal mobilization at the local level;

(G) ensuring that the Green New Deal mobilization creates high-quality union jobs that pay prevailing wages, hires local workers, offers training and advancement opportunities, and guarantees wage and benefit parity for workers affected by the transition;
(H) guaranteeing a job with a family-sustaining wage, adequate family and medical leave, paid vacations, and retirement security to all people of the United States;
(I) strengthening and protecting the right of all workers to organize, unionize, and collectively bargain free of coercion, intimidation, and harassment;
(J) strengthening and enforcing labor, workplace health and safety, antidiscrimination, and wage and hour standards across all employers, industries, and sectors;
(K) enacting and enforcing trade rules, procurement standards, and border adjustments with strong labor and environmental protections--
(i) to stop the transfer of jobs and pollution overseas; and
(ii) to grow domestic manufacturing in the United States;
(L) ensuring that public lands, waters, and oceans are protected and that eminent domain is not abused;

(M) obtaining the free, prior, and informed consent of indigenous peoples for all decisions that affect indigenous peoples and their traditional territories, honoring all treaties and agreements with indigenous peoples, and protecting and enforcing the sovereignty and land rights of indigenous peoples;
(N) ensuring a commercial environment where every businessperson is free from unfair competition and domination by domestic or international monopolies; and
(O) providing all people of the United States with--
(i) high-quality health care;
(ii) affordable, safe, and adequate housing;
(iii) economic security; and
(iv) clean water, clean air, healthy and affordable food, and access to nature.

cls.banner: The Green New Deal resolution states an opinion of the House of Representatives. Even if adopted, it would not change federal law, direct any agency or spend any money, and it would not be sent to the Senate or the President.
cls.checks: This analysis does not run its loophole, enforcement and funding checks on the Green New Deal resolution, because the resolution imposes no obligation that could be enforced. The analysis instead compares the resolution's stated goals to its legal effect and sets out what a binding version would have to contain.

stated.t: Recognizing the duty of the Federal Government to create a Green New Deal.

A new national, social, industrial, and economic mobilization on a scale not seen since World War II and the New Deal era is a historic opportunity to create millions of good, high-wage jobs, provide unprecedented levels of prosperity and economic security, and counteract systemic injustices.

marketed.t: The nonbinding resolution seeks to eliminate U.S. greenhouse gas emissions within a decade and transition the economy away from fossil fuels.
A release on the 2023 Senate reintroduction says the resolution "directs Congress to act urgently to protect the planet".
The resolution is "not a law but a nonbinding symbol of congressional sentiment".

ladder.mechanism: The resolution would put the House on record that the federal government has a duty to create a Green New Deal.
ladder.outcome: The resolution would establish a shared framework of climate and economic goals against which later bills can be measured.
ladder.aim: The resolution's stated aim is net-zero greenhouse gas emissions, millions of jobs and greater economic security, achieved through a ten-year national mobilization.

promises.p: The title of the Green New Deal resolution states that it recognizes a duty of the federal government to create a Green New Deal.
promises.why: Adoption would record the House's opinion that a federal duty to create a Green New Deal exists. A simple resolution has no power to create a legal duty.

promises.p: Paragraph (1)(A) of the Green New Deal resolution states net-zero greenhouse gas emissions as the resolution's first goal.
promises.why: Net-zero emissions is stated only as a goal. No provision of the resolution caps, prices or regulates greenhouse gas emissions, and the resolving clause gives no date for reaching net-zero.

promises.p: News coverage described the Green New Deal resolution as seeking to eliminate U.S. greenhouse gas emissions within a decade.
promises.why: Paragraph (2) of the resolving clause states that the goals "should be accomplished through a 10-year national mobilization". The resolution does not say when the ten years begin or that net-zero emissions must be reached by their end.

promises.p: A 2023 Senate press release described the Green New Deal resolution as directing Congress to act.
promises.why: A resolution expressing the sense of a chamber states an opinion. It cannot direct Congress, a committee or an agency to do anything.

promises.p: Paragraphs (1)(B) and (4)(H) of the Green New Deal resolution call for millions of good, high-wage jobs and for guaranteeing a job to all people of the United States.
promises.why: The resolution creates no program, agency, eligibility rule or funding for the jobs it describes or for the job guarantee.

promises.p: Paragraph (2)(C) of the Green New Deal resolution calls for meeting 100 percent of U.S. power demand through clean, renewable and zero-emission energy sources.
promises.why: The 100 percent clean power goal has no standard, no deadline and no definition of which energy sources qualify.

questions.q: What would be legally different the day after the House adopted the Green New Deal resolution?
questions.a: Nothing would be legally different. A simple resolution speaks for one chamber, is not sent to the Senate or the President, and has no force of law. The Congressional Research Service notes that agencies may still watch such measures as a signal of what Congress might do later.

s.l: CRS, "Sense of" Resolutions and Provisions

questions.q: For each goal in the Green New Deal resolution, which words in the resolution would deliver it?
questions.a: None of the goals is paired with an operative provision. The verbs are mostly "it is the duty", "should be accomplished" and "will require". The one "shall", in the clause on frontline and vulnerable communities, sits inside a statement of the sense of the House and binds no one. The resolution creates no agency, makes no appropriation and amends no statute.

questions.q: Even read only as a statement of goals, where does the wording of the Green New Deal resolution leave room for differing interpretations?
questions.a: Four of the resolution's emissions goals are qualified by as far as is "technologically feasible". The net-zero goal has no date in the resolving clause. The phrase "clean, renewable, and zero-emission" energy is not defined, so the resolution does not settle whether nuclear power or fossil generation with carbon capture counts.

questions.q: Which agency or official does the Green New Deal resolution assign to carry out its goals?
questions.a: The resolution assigns its duty only to "the Federal Government" as a whole. It names no department, agency, official or committee.

questions.q: What would the Green New Deal resolution cost, and where would the money come from?
questions.a: The Green New Deal resolution contains no cost figure and provides no funding. Because it has no budgetary effect, no official cost estimate would be prepared for it.

questions.q: Has the text of the Green New Deal resolution ever been voted on in Congress?
questions.a: The House has not voted on the resolution. The Senate majority leader introduced the same text as a joint resolution, and on March 26, 2019 a motion to take it up failed with 0 votes in favor, 57 against and 43 senators voting present.

s.l: Senate roll call vote 52, 116th Congress

questions.q: Do binding bills exist that would carry out parts of the Green New Deal resolution's framework?
questions.a: Binding bills of that kind exist. Sponsors have introduced separate bills, including a Green New Deal for Public Housing Act and Civilian Climate Corps legislation, and a bill to establish a Green New Deal for public schools was introduced in July 2026. Those bills, not the resolution, are the vehicles to which loophole analysis applies.

H.R. 9959, 119th Congress

questions.q: What would a binding version of the Green New Deal resolution's first goal, net-zero greenhouse gas emissions, need to contain?
questions.a: A binding net-zero measure would need a statutory emissions target with dates, a named agency with authority to set and enforce limits, a funding source, and a way to enforce the target against the government itself. The "binding version" table in the bigger picture panel sets out these requirements goal by goal.

questions.q: How does the ten-year buildout fit with the consent, land-protection and local-leadership clauses?
questions.a: Paragraph (2) calls for a 10-year mobilization that includes high-speed rail, new power capacity, grid upgrades and upgrading all existing buildings. Paragraph (4) also calls for consent of indigenous peoples for all decisions affecting them (4)(M). It calls for processes "led by frontline and vulnerable communities" at the local level (4)(F). It calls for protection of public lands, waters and oceans with eminent domain "not abused" (4)(L), and for no adverse effect on frontline and vulnerable communities (4)(B)(iii). The text does not say which goal gives way when they conflict, or how. A binding version would have to decide.

questions.q: Who would not be in a "frontline and vulnerable community"?
questions.a: Paragraph (1)(E) defines the term as a list that includes indigenous peoples, communities of color, migrant communities, deindustrialized and depopulated rural communities, the poor, low-income workers, women, the elderly, the unhoused, people with disabilities and youth. No income, place or other limit narrows the list. Because women, youth and the elderly are all included, the group is very large, so the clauses that give it priority or focus, (4)(C) and (4)(E), do not by themselves say who comes first.

questions.q: Who counts as "all people of the United States"?
questions.a: The phrase is used for the jobs, health care, housing, education and economic security goals, in paragraphs (1)(B), (1)(D), (4)(C), (4)(H) and (4)(O). The text does not say whether it means citizens, lawful residents or everyone living in the country. A binding program would need an eligibility rule.

questions.q: Which other key terms does the resolution leave undefined?
questions.a: Beyond the terms in G5 to G7, the text leaves several terms undefined. These are "fair and just transition" (1)(A), "community-defined projects and strategies" (2)(A) and (2)(I), and "smart" grids (2)(D). They also include "appropriate ownership stakes and returns on investment" and "adequate capital" (4)(A), "community ownership" (4)(E), and "family-sustaining wage" (4)(H). The list continues with "abused" for eminent domain (4)(L), "unfair competition" (4)(N), and "high-quality" health care and "affordable" housing (4)(O). The text does not say whether public ownership stakes would apply to private projects that receive public capital; the plain review suggests this could discourage private investment, a possibility the text neither confirms nor rules out. Any binding version would need definitions.

questions.q: Who speaks for a community in the processes "led by frontline and vulnerable communities"?
questions.a: The text does not say. Paragraph (4)(F) calls for "democratic and participatory processes that are inclusive of and led by frontline and vulnerable communities and workers to plan, implement, and administer the Green New Deal mobilization at the local level". It does not say how representatives are chosen, who certifies them, or who is accountable if funds administered locally are misspent.

questions.q: Would the labor standards in (4)(G) raise costs or lengthen the ten-year timeline?
questions.a: The text does not say. It sets union, prevailing-wage, local-hire and wage-parity goals in (4)(G) and a 10-year mobilization in paragraph (2), but it gives no budget or schedule against which to measure the effect. The plain review suggests the labor terms could conflict with cost and speed; that is a prediction this analysis has not verified.

questions.q: Would the border adjustments in (4)(K) be consistent with U.S. trade agreements?
questions.a: The text does not say, and it does not describe how the adjustments would work. GATT Article II:2(a) allows a charge on imports that is "equivalent to an internal tax imposed consistently with the provisions of paragraph 2 of Article III" on the like domestic product. Whether a particular adjustment fits that rule would depend on its design, which the resolution leaves to later legislation.

a.q: it is the sense of the House of Representatives

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution expresses the sense of the House of Representatives and, if adopted, would have no force of law.
findings.plain: The resolving clause of the Green New Deal resolution begins with the words "it is the sense of the House of Representatives", which mean the House is stating a view. Nothing that follows those words can require any person or agency to act, whatever the language says.
findings.tech: The Green New Deal resolution is a simple resolution, which is adopted by one chamber and is not presented to the President. The Congressional Research Service describes sense-of measures as not legally binding. Every paragraph of the resolving clause depends grammatically on the sense-of-the-House clause.
findings.use: A member of Congress can cite a vote for, or cosponsorship of, the Green New Deal resolution as action on climate even though no law has changed.

items.h: The Green New Deal resolution was introduced in the House three times and never received a House vote.
items.d: The resolution was introduced as House Resolution 109 in 2019 with 101 cosponsors, as House Resolution 332 in 2021 with 104, and as House Resolution 319 in 2023 with 96. Each version was referred to committee and went no further.

a.q: it is the duty of the Federal Government to create a Green New Deal

findings.title: Paragraph (1) of the Green New Deal resolution declares a federal duty to create a Green New Deal but assigns that duty to no agency or official.
findings.plain: The resolution states that the federal government has a duty to create a Green New Deal. It names no department, official or deadline, so no particular entity would be responsible for carrying out the duty.
findings.tech: Binding mandates name an officer, as in "the Administrator shall". The phrase "the Federal Government" in paragraph (1) does not identify an entity that can be ordered, sued or funded as such.

a.q: should be accomplished through a 10-year national mobilization

findings.title: Paragraph (2) frames the Green New Deal resolution's ten-year national mobilization with "should" and states no start date for the ten years.
findings.plain: Paragraph (2) states that the resolution's goals "should be accomplished" through a ten-year national mobilization. "Should" expresses a recommendation, and the resolution does not say when the ten years begin.
findings.tech: In drafting practice, "should" is hortatory. The phrase "10-year national mobilization" in paragraph (2) has no start date, and the 2021 and 2023 reintroductions carried the same ten-year language forward.
findings.use: Because the resolution sets no start date, a speaker can describe the ten-year timeline as beginning at any point the speaker chooses.

a.q: as much as technologically feasible
as much as is technologically feasible

findings.title: Four emissions goals in paragraph (2) of the Green New Deal resolution are qualified by the words "technologically feasible", with no designated decision-maker.
findings.plain: For infrastructure, manufacturing, agriculture and transportation, the resolution sets a goal of removing greenhouse gas emissions "as much as technologically feasible". The resolution does not say who decides what is technologically feasible.
findings.tech: In a binding statute, this qualifier hands the standard to whoever judges feasibility, and that judgment usually rests on the regulated industry's own evidence. The qualifier appears four times in the resolution, in subparagraphs (B)(i), (F), (G) and (H) of paragraph (2).
findings.use: If the qualifier were carried unchanged into a binding bill, each sector's emissions goal would be only as strong as the finding of what is technologically feasible.

a.q: net-zero greenhouse gas emissions

findings.title: Paragraph (1)(A) of the Green New Deal resolution sets a net-zero greenhouse gas emissions goal with no date, baseline or accounting method in the resolving clause.
findings.plain: The first goal in the resolution is net-zero greenhouse gas emissions. The resolution does not say by when the goal is to be reached, how emissions are measured, or what counts as an offset.
findings.tech: The preamble cites a need for net-zero global emissions by 2050. The resolving clause links the goals to a ten-year mobilization in paragraph (2) but sets no net-zero date. The word "net" implies removals or offsets, which the resolution does not define.
findings.use: Supporters and critics can each describe the net-zero target differently, and both can point to the resolution's text.

s.l: Coverage describing the goal as elimination within a decade

two.dec: Would binding legislation carrying out the Green New Deal resolution set a date for reaching net-zero greenhouse gas emissions?

views.why: Climate movement organizations would want a date for reaching net-zero emissions.

s.l: National Review

a.q: clean, renewable, and zero-emission energy sources

findings.title: Paragraph (2)(C) of the Green New Deal resolution does not specify which energy sources qualify as "clean, renewable, and zero-emission".
findings.plain: Paragraph (2)(C) calls for meeting 100 percent of the power demand in the United States from "clean, renewable, and zero-emission" energy sources. The resolution does not say whether a source must meet all three criteria or any one of them, which determines whether nuclear power qualifies.
findings.tech: Nuclear generation is zero-emission but not renewable, and fossil generation with carbon capture is arguably neither. Leaving the list of qualifying sources open can keep supporters with differing views in one coalition, which is why this finding is classified as a trade-off.
findings.use: The undefined category moves the decision about which energy sources qualify to whatever binding bill comes later.

a.q: guaranteeing a job with a family-sustaining wage

findings.title: Paragraph (4)(H) of the Green New Deal resolution refers to guaranteeing employment but establishes no program, eligibility rule or funding.
findings.plain: Paragraph (4)(H) of the resolution speaks of "guaranteeing a job" to all people of the United States. A guarantee of employment requires a program, an employer of last resort, eligibility rules and funding, and the resolution contains none of these.
findings.tech: The same is true of "guaranteeing universal access to clean water" in paragraph (2)(B)(ii) and of "providing all people of the United States with" "high-quality health care" in paragraph (4)(O). In a non-binding text, these phrases are statements of aim.
findings.use: A speaker can quote the word "guaranteeing" from the resolution as if a job guarantee had been enacted.

findings.pat: One chamber cannot bind future legislation

a.q: ensuring that any infrastructure bill considered by Congress addresses climate change

findings.title: Paragraph (2)(B)(iv) of the Green New Deal resolution calls for conditions on future infrastructure legislation that a simple resolution cannot impose.
findings.plain: Paragraph (2)(B)(iv) calls for ensuring that any infrastructure bill considered by Congress addresses climate change. A statement of opinion by one chamber cannot control the content of later bills.
findings.tech: A chamber can bind its own proceedings through its rules, for example by creating a point of order. A sense-of-the-House resolution is not a rule of the House.

a.q: Whereas the October 2018 report

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution's quantitative climate targets, such as the 1.5 degree Celsius warming limit, appear in the preamble, which has no operative effect.
findings.plain: The resolution's specific numerical targets, such as the 1.5 degree limit and the 2050 date, appear in the "Whereas" clauses. Those clauses explain why the House is speaking and are not part of what the House resolves.
findings.tech: Preambles and findings can inform interpretation but create no rights or duties. In the Green New Deal resolution, the most concrete targets appear outside the resolving clause.
findings.use: Figures from the Green New Deal resolution's preamble are often quoted as if they were commitments.

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution contains no cost estimate and no authorization or appropriation of funds for its goals.
findings.plain: The resolution names goals that would require very large public investment. It contains no cost figure and provides no funding, and a resolution could not provide funding.
findings.tech: Only a bill or joint resolution that becomes law can authorize or appropriate funds. Paragraph (4)(A) refers to "adequate capital" through community grants, public banks and other public financing, without stating amounts.
findings.use: Cost estimates for the Green New Deal from supporters and opponents cannot be checked against the resolution, because the resolution contains none.

findings.pat: Vote taken on a different vehicle
findings.title: The House did not vote on the Green New Deal resolution, and the Senate vote on a companion joint resolution failed 0 to 57.
findings.plain: The House never voted on the Green New Deal resolution. The Senate held a procedural vote on the same text, introduced by the majority leader, and it failed 0 to 57, with 43 senators voting present.
findings.tech: Senate Joint Resolution 8 carried the same text as a joint resolution. Supporters of the House resolution called the vote a tactic and voted present. The episode shows how a non-binding text can be used to put members on record.
findings.use: Either side can cite the Senate vote on the Green New Deal text, one as proof of no support and the other as proof of a sham process.

findings.title: Separate bills introduced under the Green New Deal name, unlike House Resolution 109 itself, would carry binding provisions if enacted.
findings.plain: Readers looking for measures that would change federal law should look to the separate bills introduced under the Green New Deal name, such as those on public housing and a Civilian Climate Corps.
findings.tech: Those companion measures are bills (H.R. and S.), which would be binding if enacted and can be red-teamed for loopholes in the ordinary way.

s.l: Green New Deal for Public Housing Act reintroduction
2023 reintroduction with companion legislation

a.q: obtaining the free, prior, and informed consent of indigenous peoples for all decisions that affect indigenous peoples and their traditional territories

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution calls for indigenous consent to all affecting decisions, a stronger standard than the consultation the federal government has committed to.
findings.plain: Paragraph (4)(M) says a Green New Deal will require getting the consent of indigenous peoples for every decision that affects them or their traditional lands. Current federal practice asks agencies to consult tribes and get their input. When the United States endorsed the United Nations declaration on indigenous rights in 2010, it said it read consent to mean meaningful consultation, not necessarily agreement. The resolution does not say which of these two meanings it uses.
findings.tech: Paragraph (4)(M) of the resolved clause lists "obtaining the free, prior, and informed consent of indigenous peoples for all decisions that affect indigenous peoples and their traditional territories" among the things a Green New Deal "will require". Section 5(a) of Executive Order 13175 requires that "Each agency shall have an accountable process to ensure meaningful and timely input by tribal officials in the development of regulatory policies that have tribal implications". The 2010 State Department announcement of United States support for the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples states that the United States "recognizes the significance of the Declaration's provisions on free, prior and informed consent". It adds that it understands them "to call for a process of meaningful consultation with tribal leaders, but not necessarily the agreement of those leaders, before the actions addressed in those consultations are taken". The resolution uses the Declaration's phrase without adopting or rejecting that reading. It applies the phrase to "all decisions", not only regulatory policies. Being a sense-of resolution, it changes neither the order nor the United States interpretation. The gap matters for any binding bill that carries the phrase forward.
findings.use: Supporters can cite the phrase as a commitment to a consent standard, while an agency could treat the same phrase as satisfied by the consultation it already conducts.

s.l: Executive Order 13175, Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments (2000)
U.S. Department of State, Announcement of U.S. Support for the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2010)

a.q: ensuring that frontline and vulnerable communities shall not be adversely affected

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution states that frontline and vulnerable communities "shall not be adversely affected", the only "shall" in the resolved clause, with no balancing test.
findings.plain: Paragraph (4)(B)(iii) says frontline and vulnerable communities "shall not be adversely affected". This is an all-or-nothing standard: it does not say how much harm is acceptable or how harm is weighed against benefits. It is also the only place in the resolved clause that uses "shall", but because the whole clause is the House's opinion, the word does not make it binding.
findings.tech: Clause (4)(B)(iii) reads "ensuring that frontline and vulnerable communities shall not be adversely affected". It is the only occurrence of "shall" in the text. It sits under "it is the sense of the House of Representatives that", so it carries no force (see G1). The standard is unqualified: no threshold of harm, no net-benefit test and no decision-maker. Read with paragraph (1)(E), the protected class is the full list of groups in the definition of "frontline and vulnerable communities", so taken literally the standard would reach any project with a local adverse effect on any member of those groups.
findings.use: If carried into a binding bill unchanged, the clause could be cited against nearly any project with a local cost; a drafter would need to add a threshold or a balancing test.

a.q: (A) global reductions in greenhouse gas emissions from human sources of 40 to 60 percent from 2010 levels by 2030; and

findings.title: The Green New Deal preamble presents IPCC carbon dioxide figures, a 40 to 60 percent cut by 2030 and net zero by 2050, as figures for all greenhouse gases.
findings.plain: The preamble says the world must cut greenhouse gas emissions 40 to 60 percent from 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net-zero emissions by 2050. The IPCC report it cites gives those numbers for carbon dioxide only, with a central estimate of about 45 percent. For other gases such as methane, the report describes deep cuts, not net zero by 2050.
findings.tech: Preamble paragraph (4) cites the IPCC Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5 °C for "global reductions in greenhouse gas emissions from human sources of 40 to 60 percent from 2010 levels by 2030" and "net-zero global emissions by 2050". SPM paragraph C.1 states that in pathways with no or limited overshoot "global net anthropogenic CO2 emissions decline by about 45% from 2010 levels by 2030", with an interquartile range of 40 to 60 percent. It adds "reaching net zero around 2050", with an interquartile range of 2045 to 2055. For other gases it states the following. "Non-CO2 emissions in pathways that limit global warming to 1.5°C show deep reductions that are similar to those in pathways limiting warming to 2°C". C.1.2 gives methane and black carbon reductions of "35% or more of both by 2050 relative to 2010". The preamble therefore reports the CO2 interquartile range as a greenhouse gas range and drops the 45 percent central estimate. The preamble has no operative effect (G12), so this affects how the case is framed, not what the resolution does.
findings.use: Critics can point out the mismatch with the cited report; supporters can cite the same report for the CO2 figures as stated there.

s.l: IPCC, Global Warming of 1.5 °C, Summary for Policymakers (2018)

a.q: (F) a risk of damage to $1,000,000,000,000 of public infrastructure and coastal real estate in the United States; and

findings.title: The Green New Deal preamble treats $1 trillion of coastal property risk as a result of 2 degrees of warming, though the cited assessment calls it a present risk.
findings.plain: The preamble lists a risk of damage to $1 trillion of public infrastructure and coastal real estate among the effects of warming at or above 2 degrees Celsius. The Fourth National Climate Assessment, which the preamble cites, says rising seas "now threaten" about $1 trillion in coastal real estate. It describes a current risk, not one tied to 2 degrees of warming.
findings.tech: Preamble paragraph (3) attributes items (A) to (F) to "global warming at or above 2 degrees Celsius beyond preindustrialized levels". NCA4 Volume II, Chapter 8, states: "Although storms, floods, and erosion have always been hazards, in combination with rising sea levels they now threaten approximately $1 trillion in national wealth held in coastal real estate". The chapter summary refers to "America's trillion-dollar coastal property market and public infrastructure" as threatened. Neither passage ties the figure to a warming level, scenario or date. The companion figure in item (B), more than $500 billion in lost annual output by 2100, could not be located in the NCA4 text read (see rejected points), so it is not addressed here.
findings.use: The figure can be cited accurately as a present-day exposure; citing it as a consequence of 2 degrees of warming goes beyond the source.

s.l: Fourth National Climate Assessment, Volume II, Chapter 8: Coastal Effects

a.q: a large racial wealth divide amounting to a difference of 20 times more wealth between the average white family and the average black family

findings.title: The Green New Deal preamble describes the 20 times racial wealth gap as a gap between average families, while the known source for that figure measured median household wealth.
findings.plain: The preamble says the average white family has 20 times more wealth than the average black family. The Pew Research Center study that reported a 20 times gap compared median wealth, the wealth of the household in the middle, using 2009 data. An average and a median can give very different ratios.
findings.tech: Preamble clause on income inequality, item (B): "a difference of 20 times more wealth between the average white family and the average black family". The resolution gives no source for this item. Pew Research Center (July 26, 2011) states: "The median wealth of white households is 20 times that of black households", based on "newly available government data from 2009." The ratio is a median ratio; the preamble's "average" wording does not match it. The resolution's own next item uses "at the median" for the gender earnings gap, so the text distinguishes the two terms elsewhere.
findings.use: A critic can cite the wording as inaccurate; the underlying Pew figure supports the claim when stated as a median.

s.l: Pew Research Center, Wealth Gaps Rise to Record Highs Between Whites, Blacks, Hispanics (2011)

findings.pat: Named means narrower than the goal

a.q: removing greenhouse gases from the atmosphere and reducing pollution by restoring natural ecosystems through proven low-tech solutions that increase soil carbon storage, such as land preservation and afforestation

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution names only low-tech natural methods for removing greenhouse gases, while the IPCC report it cites lists engineered removal methods as well.
findings.plain: The net-zero goal depends on removing some greenhouse gases from the air. The only removal methods the resolution names are natural ones, such as protecting land and planting forests. The IPCC report cited in the preamble says all of its 1.5 degree pathways with little or no overshoot use carbon dioxide removal, and lists engineered methods alongside forests. The resolution neither includes nor rules out those methods.
findings.tech: Paragraph (2)(J) refers to "proven low-tech solutions that increase soil carbon storage, such as land preservation and afforestation". Paragraph (2)(M) ("identifying other emission and pollution sources and creating solutions to remove them") addresses sources, not atmospheric removal. IPCC SR1.5 SPM C.3: "All pathways that limit global warming to 1.5°C with limited or no overshoot project the use of carbon dioxide removal (CDR)" on the order of 100 to 1000 GtCO2 over the 21st century. C.3.1: "Existing and potential CDR measures include afforestation and reforestation," and the same paragraph goes on to list bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), direct air carbon capture and storage, enhanced weathering and ocean alkalinization. Together with G6 (no rule on what counts toward "net"), the text leaves the role of engineered removal open.
findings.use: Advocates for and against engineered removal can each read the resolution as consistent with their position.

s.l: IPCC, Global Warming of 1.5 °C, Summary for Policymakers (2018)

a.q: more than $500,000,000,000 in lost annual economic output in the United States by the year 2100

findings.title: The Green New Deal preamble ties $500 billion in yearly U.S. losses by 2100 to 2 degrees of warming; the cited assessment links large losses to high emissions.
findings.plain: The preamble lists more than $500 billion in lost yearly economic output by 2100 among the effects of warming at or above 2 degrees Celsius. The Fourth National Climate Assessment, which the preamble cites, says losses in some sectors could reach hundreds of billions of dollars a year by the end of the century if warming continues without significant cuts in emissions. The plain review states that losses of this size come mainly from a high-emissions scenario rather than from 2 degrees of warming. The exact $500 billion figure was not found in the assessment pages read.
findings.tech: Preamble paragraph (3) attributes items (A) to (F) to "global warming at or above 2 degrees Celsius beyond preindustrialized levels"; item (B) is "more than $500,000,000,000 in lost annual economic output in the United States by the year 2100". NCA4 Volume II Summary Findings refer to "the continued warming that is projected to occur without significant reductions in global greenhouse gas emissions". They state: "The potential for losses in some sectors could reach hundreds of billions of dollars per year by the end of this century." Contemporary reporting on the assessment (TechCrunch) quotes it as saying: "Under scenarios with high emissions and limited or no adaptation, annual losses in some sectors are estimated" to grow to "hundreds of billions of dollars by the end of the century". The same reporting summarizes the total as "nearly half a trillion dollars annually by 2090". Chapter 29 gives sector figures (for example "$155 billion in lost wages per year by 2090") but no cross-sector total on the page read. So the assessment frames large losses as a high-emissions, end-of-century result, not as a 2 degree threshold. The $500 billion number and its scenario were not located in the primary text. This point has not been verified against a primary source.
findings.use: Critics can say the preamble attaches a high-emissions figure to a 2 degree threshold; supporters can cite the assessment's own language on losses of hundreds of billions of dollars a year.

s.l: Fourth National Climate Assessment, Volume II, Summary Findings
Fourth National Climate Assessment, Volume II, Chapter 29: Reducing Risks Through Emissions Mitigation
TechCrunch on the Fourth National Climate Assessment, Volume II (2018)

a.q: the top 1 percent of earners accruing 91 percent of gains in the first few years of economic recovery after the Great Recession

findings.title: The Green New Deal preamble's 91 percent figure for top earners covers the first three recovery years; the same source later put the six-year share at 52 percent.
findings.plain: The preamble says the top 1 percent of earners received 91 percent of income gains in the first few years after the Great Recession. That matches economist Emmanuel Saez's estimate for 2009 to 2012. His later update, covering 2009 to 2015, found the top 1 percent received 52 percent of the gains over the first six years. The preamble's figure is accurate for the period it names, but the share shrank as the recovery went on.
findings.tech: The preamble clause on income inequality, item (A), draws on Saez, updated with 2015 estimates. He wrote: "Hence, the top 1% captured 91% of the income gains in the first three years of the recovery." He also wrote: "Hence, the top 1% captured 52% of the income gains in the first six years of the recovery." The resolution's wording ("the first few years") is consistent with the three-year figure. The plain review describes the figure as later revised; the source shows instead that the longer period gives a lower share. The preamble has no operative effect (G12).
findings.use: Both sides can cite the same source: the three-year figure supports the preamble, and the six-year figure shows the share declined.

s.l: Emmanuel Saez, Striking it Richer: The Evolution of Top Incomes in the United States (updated with 2015 estimates)

a.q: life expectancy declining

findings.title: The Green New Deal preamble describes U.S. life expectancy as declining, which matched data through 2017; the CDC later reported a small increase for 2018.
findings.plain: The preamble lists declining life expectancy among current crises. When the resolution was introduced in February 2019, the latest final data showed life expectancy falling to 78.6 years in 2017. The CDC later reported that it rose to 78.7 years in 2018. The statement was accurate when written but describes a condition that changed.
findings.tech: Preamble, crises clause, paragraph (1): "life expectancy declining". CDC Data Brief 328: "Life expectancy for the U.S. population declined to 78.6 years in 2017". CDC Data Brief 355: "Life expectancy for the U.S. population in 2018 was 78.7 years, an increase of 0.1 year from 2017." The resolution states a dated condition in the present tense; later reintroductions would need current figures. The preamble has no operative effect (G12).
findings.use: Anyone quoting the preamble today should give the year of the data it reflects.

s.l: CDC National Center for Health Statistics, Data Brief No. 328, Mortality in the United States, 2017
CDC National Center for Health Statistics, Data Brief No. 355, Mortality in the United States, 2018

a.q: having emitted 20 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions through 2014

findings.title: The Green New Deal preamble says the United States emitted 20 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions through 2014 without naming a source, start year or which gases count.
findings.plain: The preamble says the United States has emitted 20 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions through 2014. It does not say where the number comes from, what year the count starts, or whether it covers only carbon dioxide or all gases and land use. Published estimates of historical responsibility differ depending on those choices. One widely reported study put the U.S. share of warming at about 20 percent from 1750 to 2005, counting several gases and land use.
findings.tech: Preamble: "having emitted 20 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions through 2014". No source, baseline year, gas coverage or land-use treatment is given. Carbon Brief reports a 2014 study. It states "The United States is responsible for a whopping 20 per cent of the warming" and that the study "examined each country's greenhouse gas emissions between 1750 and 2005". The study counted "carbon dioxide from fossil fuel burning and land use change, they included methane, nitrous oxide and sulphate aerosol emissions." That figure is a share of warming over a different period, not a share of emissions through 2014, so the preamble's exact metric could not be matched. The preamble has no operative effect (G12).
findings.use: Critics and supporters can each cite estimates with different metrics; the text gives no basis to choose among them.

s.l: Carbon Brief, UK tops list of world's biggest greenhouse gas emitters (2014)

a.q: the third-worst level of socioeconomic mobility in the developed world before the Great Recession

findings.title: The Green New Deal preamble ranks the United States third-worst in socioeconomic mobility in the developed world without naming the study or the countries compared.
findings.plain: The preamble says the United States had the third-worst socioeconomic mobility in the developed world before the Great Recession. It names no source. Fact-checkers have traced a similar claim to a 2010 OECD study that placed the United States 10th of 12 developed countries, which fits "third-worst". They also note that the exact ranking depends on which countries are included.
findings.tech: Preamble, crises clause, paragraph (2)(B). PolitiFact (2013), on a comparable claim, states the research "did find the U.S. to be 10th among the 12 examined countries", that "those 12 were all developed countries", and that "America's exact ranking in those studies depends on which countries are surveyed." The measure it describes is the share of fathers' earnings advantage passed to sons: "at least 40 percent of the economic advantage that high-earning fathers have over low-earning fathers". The plain review says the ranking also depends on the measure used; the source read addresses only the choice of countries. The preamble has no operative effect (G12).
findings.use: The ranking can be cited with its source and sample; without them, a critic can point to other samples with a different rank.

s.l: PolitiFact, Rep. Tim Ryan says United States ranks behind other countries in social mobility (2013)

findings.pat: Undefined limit on an existing power

a.q: eminent domain is not abused

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution says eminent domain should not be "abused" without defining abuse, while federal law lets approved transmission lines take land by eminent domain.
findings.plain: Paragraph (4)(L) says a Green New Deal will require that eminent domain is not abused. It does not say what counts as abuse. The resolution also calls for new transmission, grid and rail projects over ten years. Under existing federal law, the holder of a federal permit for certain transmission lines may take the right-of-way by eminent domain when it cannot reach agreement with the owner, so a binding version would have to say how the two fit together.
findings.tech: (4)(L): "ensuring that public lands, waters, and oceans are protected and that eminent domain is not abused". "Abused" is undefined and no standard or decision-maker is named. Federal Power Act section 216(e)(1), 16 U.S.C. 824p(e)(1), provides that for permits under subsection (b) "the permit holder may acquire the right-of-way by the exercise of the right of eminent domain" when it cannot acquire it by contract or agree on compensation. The Natural Gas Act, 15 U.S.C. 717f(h), gives a similar power to pipeline certificate holders: "it may acquire the same by the exercise of the right of eminent domain in the district court of the United States". Paragraph (2)(D) calls for "building or upgrading to energy-efficient, distributed, and \"smart\" power grids" and (2)(H)(iii) for "high-speed rail". The resolution does not say whether use of these existing powers for Green New Deal projects would be a permitted use or an abuse. Being a sense-of resolution, it changes neither statute.
findings.use: Landowners and project opponents could read "not abused" as a limit on condemnation for new lines; developers could read it as consistent with condemnation under existing procedures.

s.l: 16 U.S.C. 824p, Siting of interstate electric transmission facilities
15 U.S.C. 717f, Natural Gas Act certificates

findings.pat: Unstated input to a stated goal

a.q: to stop the transfer of jobs and pollution overseas

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution does not address the minerals its clean power and vehicle goals would require, though its trade, land and consent clauses bear on their sourcing.
findings.plain: The resolution calls for 100 percent clean power and zero-emission vehicle infrastructure, but it never mentions mining or minerals. The International Energy Agency reports that a typical electric car needs six times the mineral inputs of a conventional car. Mining at home could run into the clauses on protecting public lands and on indigenous consent, while importing could run into the goal of stopping the transfer of jobs and pollution overseas. The text does not say how to weigh these.
findings.tech: Goals: (2)(C) "meeting 100 percent of the power demand in the United States through clean, renewable, and zero-emission energy sources"; (2)(H)(i) "zero-emission vehicle infrastructure and manufacturing". Constraints: (4)(K)(i) "to stop the transfer of jobs and pollution overseas"; (4)(L) protection of "public lands, waters, and oceans"; (4)(M) consent of indigenous peoples. The words "mining" and "mineral" do not appear. The IEA (2021) states: "A typical electric car requires six times the mineral inputs of a conventional car"; "an onshore wind plant requires nine times more mineral resources than a similarly sized gas-fired power plant". It also states that energy-sector mineral needs "could increase by as much as six times by 2040" in climate-driven scenarios. Whether domestic mining or imports would in fact conflict with (4)(K) to (4)(M) depends on project facts the text does not reach. The conflict is stated here as a possibility.
findings.use: Opponents can point to the missing supply plan; supporters can argue (4)(K) and (4)(L) set conditions on sourcing rather than forbid it.

s.l: International Energy Agency, Clean energy demand for critical minerals set to soar as the world pursues net zero goals (2021)

a.q: labor unions, worker cooperatives, civil society groups, academia, and businesses

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution names development partners who would also benefit from its terms and sets no conflict-of-interest, audit or bidding rules for its envisioned funds.
findings.plain: Paragraph (3) says a Green New Deal must be developed in partnership with groups including labor unions, worker cooperatives, civil society groups and businesses. Several of these would also benefit from other paragraphs, such as the union-job terms in (4)(G) and the capital and grants in (4)(A). The resolution has no rule separating advisory roles from receiving money, and no provision on audits, inspectors general, competitive bidding or fraud. Because it is non-binding and spends nothing, these gaps have no effect now, but any implementing law would need to address them.
findings.tech: (3): "a Green New Deal must be developed through transparent and inclusive consultation, collaboration, and partnership with frontline and vulnerable communities, labor unions, worker cooperatives, civil society groups, academia, and businesses". (4)(A): "adequate capital (including through community grants, public banks, and other public financing)" to "communities, organizations, Federal, State, and local government agencies, and businesses working on the Green New Deal mobilization". (4)(G): "high-quality union jobs". (2)(A) and (2)(I): "community-defined projects and strategies". The only process value stated is "transparent and inclusive". No text addresses recusal, conflicts of interest, audits, competitive award or recovery of misspent funds. The analysis notes elsewhere that no funds or duties exist to misuse, in its description of the checks applied; this finding records what the text would carry into a binding version.
findings.use: Critics can cite the overlap of partners and recipients; drafters of binding bills can treat the list as the set of parties needing conflict rules.

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution combines climate goals with commitments on jobs, health care, housing, education, labor law, trade and monopolies in one statement.
findings.plain: Alongside its climate goals, the resolution includes a job guarantee, high-quality health care and housing for all, education including higher education, stronger labor rights, trade rules and freedom from monopolies. Each is a large policy area in its own right. Because they are in one text, a vote for or against the resolution does not show a position on any single item, and the climate parts cannot be weighed on their own.
findings.tech: Paragraph (4) holds these non-climate items. Item (C) reads "high-quality education, including higher education, to all people of the United States". Item (H) reads "guaranteeing a job with a family-sustaining wage, adequate family and medical leave, paid vacations, and retirement security". Item (I) names the right "to organize, unionize, and collectively bargain". Item (J) covers labor, safety, antidiscrimination and wage standards "across all employers, industries, and sectors". Item (K) reads "trade rules, procurement standards, and border adjustments". Item (N) names freedom "from unfair competition and domination by domestic or international monopolies". Item (O) names "high-quality health care", "affordable, safe, and adequate housing" and "economic security". The preamble links them to the climate goals through "systemic injustices". Combining them is a deliberate choice that builds a coalition around one framework, so it is labeled a trade-off. G8 addresses the job guarantee alone.
findings.use: Supporters can present the whole agenda as one program; opponents can cite any single item as a reason to oppose the whole.

a.q: creates high-quality union jobs that pay prevailing wages

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution calls for union jobs without saying how this applies to non-union contractors or in states that bar union-membership requirements.
findings.plain: Paragraph (4)(G) says the mobilization should create high-quality union jobs paying prevailing wages. It does not say whether non-union contractors could do the work. Federal labor law lets states prohibit agreements that make union membership a condition of employment, which is what right-to-work laws do. The resolution does not say how its union-jobs goal would work in those states.
findings.tech: (4)(G): "ensuring that the Green New Deal mobilization creates high-quality union jobs that pay prevailing wages, hires local workers, offers training and advancement opportunities, and guarantees wage and benefit parity for workers affected by the transition". National Labor Relations Act section 14(b), 29 U.S.C. 164(b), provides the following. "Nothing in this subchapter shall be construed as authorizing the execution or application of agreements requiring membership in a labor organization as a condition of employment in any State or Territory in which such execution or application is prohibited by State or Territorial law." The resolution does not say whether "union jobs" means work under a collective bargaining agreement, a project labor agreement, or union membership by each worker. It also says nothing about non-union contractors. (4)(I) separately calls for "strengthening and protecting the right of all workers to organize", which a binding bill could pursue by amending federal law.
findings.use: Unions can read (4)(G) as favoring union contractors; non-union contractors and right-to-work states can read it as compatible with open bidding.

s.l: 29 U.S.C. 164, National Labor Relations Act section 14

bigger.lead: The Green New Deal resolution names nearly every part of the federal climate and economic agenda. Because the resolution has no legal effect, it changes none of them. The first table shows what the resolution names, and the second table shows what a binding measure would need for each goal.

map.note: The resolution states net-zero emissions as a goal and sets no cap, price or standard for greenhouse gas emissions.
The resolution calls for 100 percent clean, renewable and zero-emission power and does not define which sources qualify.
The goals for infrastructure, industry, agriculture and transportation are qualified by technological feasibility. The goal for upgrading buildings is not.
The resolution states no amounts or sources for public investment and financing.
The resolution states guarantees for jobs, wages and labor rights without creating programs to deliver them.

map.part: Health care, housing and economic security
map.note: The resolution lists health care, housing and economic security as things a Green New Deal will require.
Later spending and tax law on clean energy was enacted through separate bills, which sponsors of the 2023 reintroduction of the resolution cited.

s.l: Sen. Wyden release on the 2023 reintroduction

map.note: The resolution has no permitting or environmental review provision. Clause (4)(L) only says eminent domain should not be abused.
The resolution does not mention mining or minerals.
Paragraph (2)(N) promotes international exchange and leadership. The resolution does not name the Paris Agreement.
Clause (4)(K) calls for trade rules and border adjustments without saying how they would work.
Clause (4)(M) uses a consent standard, while current executive practice is consultation (finding G15).
(2)(D) calls for building or upgrading grids and affordable access to electricity; reliability during the transition and interconnection backlogs are not mentioned.

map.part: Natural gas as a transition fuel
map.note: Natural gas is not mentioned; G7 covers nuclear power and carbon capture.

map.part: Fossil-fuel revenue of states, tribes and localities
map.note: No provision on the loss of fossil-fuel taxes or royalties; (4)(E) prioritizes investment in communities that may struggle with the transition.
(4)(C) calls for resources, training and education; the text does not address whether enough trained workers exist for a ten-year timeline.
(2)(F) and (4)(K)(ii) call for growing domestic and renewable energy manufacturing; dependence on foreign solar panels and batteries is not mentioned.

map.part: Relocation of communities that cannot be protected in place
map.note: (2)(A) and (2)(B)(iii) address resiliency and climate risk; relocation is not mentioned.

The preamble's targets are global and (2)(N) aims to help other countries achieve a Green New Deal; the text does not explain how U.S. action connects to the global figures. EPA data show the United States produced about 15 percent of global emissions in 2014.

s.l: U.S. EPA, Global Greenhouse Gas Emissions Data (archived January 2021)

binding.need: A statutory target with dates and interim milestones; an agency with authority to set and enforce limits; a rule for what counts as an offset; a consequence if a milestone is missed.
A definition of qualifying sources; a standard that applies to utilities; a compliance schedule; penalties or alternative compliance payments.
A program and administering agency; eligibility and wage rules; an appropriation or mandatory funding stream.
Authorized programs with appropriations; standards; a delivery mechanism through States, localities or direct federal work.
Enforceable criteria for which communities qualify; a required share of investment; reporting and a right to challenge allocations.
