cls.function: Statement of opinion by the House
cls.banner: The Green New Deal resolution states an opinion of the House of Representatives. It is not a law. Even if the House approved it, no law would change. It would not order any agency to act or spend any money. It would also not go to the Senate or the President.
cls.checks: This analysis does not check the Green New Deal resolution for loopholes, enforcement or funding. The reason is that the resolution does not make anyone do anything. Instead, the analysis compares the resolution's goals with what it would really do. It also shows what a version with the force of law would need.

stated.t: Recognizing the duty of the Federal Government to create a Green New Deal.

A new national, social, industrial, and economic mobilization on a scale not seen since World War II and the New Deal era is a historic opportunity to create millions of good, high-wage jobs, provide unprecedented levels of prosperity and economic security, and counteract systemic injustices.

marketed.t: The nonbinding resolution seeks to eliminate U.S. greenhouse gas emissions within a decade and transition the economy away from fossil fuels.
A release on the 2023 Senate reintroduction says the resolution "directs Congress to act urgently to protect the planet".
The resolution is "not a law but a nonbinding symbol of congressional sentiment".

ladder.mechanism: The Green New Deal resolution would put the House on record. The House would be saying that the federal government has a duty to create a Green New Deal.
ladder.outcome: The Green New Deal resolution would give later bills a shared set of climate and economic goals. Those bills could then be measured against the goals.
ladder.aim: The Green New Deal resolution aims for net-zero greenhouse gas emissions. It also aims for millions of jobs and more economic security. It would reach these goals through a ten-year national effort.

promises.p: The title of the Green New Deal resolution says the federal government has a duty to create a Green New Deal.
promises.why: If the House approved the Green New Deal resolution, it would record the House's opinion that this duty exists. But a statement of opinion by the House has no power to create a legal duty.

promises.p: The first goal of the Green New Deal resolution is net-zero greenhouse gas emissions.
promises.why: In the Green New Deal resolution, net-zero emissions is only a goal. Nothing in the resolution limits, prices or controls emissions. The part that says what the House resolves gives no date for net-zero.

promises.p: News reports said the Green New Deal resolution was meant to end the country's greenhouse gas emissions in ten years.
promises.why: The Green New Deal resolution says its goals "should be accomplished through a 10-year national mobilization". That means a ten-year effort across the country. But the resolution does not say when the ten years start. It also does not say net-zero must be reached by the end of them.

promises.p: A 2023 Senate press release said the Green New Deal resolution would direct Congress to act.
promises.why: The Green New Deal resolution is an opinion of one chamber of Congress, the House. A statement like that cannot order Congress, a committee or a government agency to do anything.

promises.p: The Green New Deal resolution calls for millions of good jobs with high wages. It also calls for guaranteeing a job to everyone in the United States.
promises.why: The Green New Deal resolution sets up no program or agency for these jobs. It has no rules for who qualifies. It sets aside no money for the jobs or for the job guarantee.

promises.p: The Green New Deal resolution calls for meeting 100 percent of the country's power needs. That power would come from clean, renewable and zero-emission energy sources.
promises.why: The Green New Deal goal of 100 percent clean power has no standard and no deadline. The resolution also does not list which power sources count.

questions.q: What would legally change the day after the House approved the Green New Deal resolution?
questions.a: Nothing would legally change. The Green New Deal resolution speaks only for the House. It is not sent to the Senate or the President, and it is not a law. The Congressional Research Service is a research office that works for Congress. It notes that agencies may still watch such statements as a hint of what Congress might do later.

s.l: CRS, "Sense of" Resolutions and Provisions

questions.q: Which words in the Green New Deal resolution would actually make each of its goals happen?
questions.a: No goal in the resolution comes with a way to carry it out. The verbs are mostly "it is the duty", "should be accomplished" and "will require". The one "shall" is in the part about frontline and vulnerable communities. It sits inside a statement of what the House thinks, so it binds no one. The resolution sets up no agency, spends no money and changes no law.

questions.q: Where does the wording of the Green New Deal resolution leave room for different readings of its goals?
questions.a: Four of the Green New Deal resolution's emissions goals apply only as far as is "technologically feasible". That means as far as technology makes possible. The net-zero goal has no date in the part that says what the House resolves. The resolution does not define "clean, renewable, and zero-emission" energy. So it does not settle whether nuclear power counts. It also does not settle whether fossil fuel power plants that capture their carbon count.

questions.q: Who does the Green New Deal resolution put in charge of reaching its goals?
questions.a: The Green New Deal resolution gives its duty only to "the Federal Government" as a whole. It does not name a department, an agency, an official or a committee to do the work.

questions.q: What would the Green New Deal resolution cost, and where would the money come from?
questions.a: The Green New Deal resolution gives no cost figure and provides no money. It would not spend anything. So no official cost estimate would be made for it.

questions.q: Has the text of the Green New Deal resolution ever been voted on in Congress?
questions.a: The House never voted on the Green New Deal resolution. The Senate majority leader, who leads the larger party in the Senate, brought the same text there. On March 26, 2019, a vote to take it up failed. The count was 0 in favor and 57 against, and 43 senators voted present.

s.l: Senate roll call vote 52, 116th Congress

questions.q: Have bills been introduced that would turn parts of the Green New Deal into law if they passed?
questions.a: Yes, separate bills like that have been introduced under the Green New Deal name. They include a Green New Deal for Public Housing Act and bills for a Civilian Climate Corps. A bill for a Green New Deal for public schools was introduced in July 2026. A search for loopholes applies to those bills, not to the resolution.

s.l: Reintroduction of the Green New Deal for Public Housing Act
H.R. 9959, 119th Congress

questions.q: What would a law need to actually reach the Green New Deal resolution's first goal of net-zero emissions?
questions.a: A law to reach the Green New Deal goal of net-zero emissions would need several things. It would need an emissions target with dates, written into law. It would need a named agency with power to set and enforce limits. It would need a source of money. It would also need a way to hold the government itself to the target. A table in the bigger picture panel lists these needs for each goal.

questions.q: How does the ten-year building plan fit with the goals on consent, protecting land and local leadership?
questions.a: The resolution calls for a 10-year mobilization. It includes high-speed rail, new power capacity, grid upgrades and upgrading all existing buildings. It also calls for consent of indigenous peoples for all decisions affecting them. It calls for local processes "led by frontline and vulnerable communities". It calls for protecting public lands, waters and oceans, with eminent domain "not abused". It also says those communities should not be harmed. The text does not say which goal gives way when they conflict, or how. A binding version would have to decide.

questions.q: Who would not be in a "frontline and vulnerable community"?
questions.a: The resolution defines the term as a list. The list names indigenous peoples, communities of color, migrant communities and the poor. It also names low-income workers, women, the elderly, the unhoused, people with disabilities and youth. It names deindustrialized and depopulated rural communities too. No income level or place narrows the list. Women, youth and the elderly are all on it, so the group is very large. The goals that give this group priority do not say who comes first.

questions.q: Who counts as "all people of the United States"?
questions.a: The resolution uses the phrase for its goals on jobs, health care, housing, education and economic security. The text does not say if it means citizens, lawful residents or everyone in the country. A binding program would need a rule on who can take part.

questions.q: Which other key terms does the resolution leave undefined?
questions.a: The resolution leaves many terms undefined. Examples are "fair and just transition", "smart" grids and "community ownership". Others are "family-sustaining wage", "high-quality" health care and "affordable" housing. It also leaves out "adequate capital" and "abused" for eminent domain. The text does not say if public ownership stakes would apply to private projects that get public money. The plain review says this could scare off private investment. The text neither confirms nor rules that out. Any binding version would need definitions.

questions.q: Who speaks for local groups when plans are "led by frontline and vulnerable communities"?
questions.a: The text does not say. It calls for "democratic and participatory processes" that are "led by frontline and vulnerable communities and workers". These would "plan, implement, and administer the Green New Deal mobilization at the local level". The text does not say how representatives are chosen or who certifies them. It also does not say who is accountable if money run locally is misspent.

questions.q: Would the labor standards in the resolution raise costs or lengthen its ten-year timeline?
questions.a: The text does not say. It sets goals on union jobs, prevailing wages, local hiring and wage parity. It also calls for a 10-year mobilization. It gives no budget or schedule to measure the effect against. The plain review says the labor terms could clash with cost and speed. This analysis has not verified that prediction.

questions.q: Would the resolution's border adjustments be consistent with U.S. trade agreements?
questions.a: The text does not say, and it does not describe how the adjustments would work. GATT Article II:2(a) allows a charge on imports that is "equivalent to an internal tax". The charge must be "imposed consistently with" the rules in paragraph 2 of Article III. It applies to the like domestic product. Whether an adjustment fits that rule would depend on its design. The resolution leaves the design to later legislation.

s.l: WTO Analytical Index, GATT 1994 Article II

a.q: it is the sense of the House of Representatives

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution is a statement of opinion. It would not change any law.
findings.plain: The Green New Deal resolution says "it is the sense of the House of Representatives". Those words mean the House is giving its opinion. Nothing that comes after them can make anyone do anything. That is true no matter what the rest of the wording says.
findings.tech: The Green New Deal resolution is a type of measure that only the House votes on. It never goes to the President. The Congressional Research Service, a research office of Congress, says opinion statements like this are not legally binding. That means no one has to follow them. Every goal in the resolution falls under its opening words, which state the House's opinion.
findings.use: A member of Congress can say that voting for or cosponsoring the Green New Deal resolution is action on climate. Yet no law has changed.

s.l: CRS, "Sense of" Resolutions and Provisions

a.q: it is the duty of the Federal Government to create a Green New Deal

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution says the federal government has a duty to act. It puts no one in charge.
findings.plain: The Green New Deal resolution says the federal government has a duty to create a Green New Deal. It does not name a department, an official or a deadline. So no one in particular would be in charge of that duty.
findings.tech: Laws that require action always name a specific official. For example, a law may say "the Administrator shall" act, which means that official must act. The Green New Deal resolution names only "the Federal Government" as a whole. The whole government cannot be ordered, sued or given money as one body.

a.q: should be accomplished through a 10-year national mobilization

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution only says its goals "should" be met in ten years. It sets no start date.
findings.plain: The Green New Deal resolution says its goals "should be accomplished" through a ten-year national effort. "Should" is a suggestion, not an order. The resolution also does not say when the ten years begin.
findings.tech: When laws are written, "should" suggests an action but does not require it. The phrase "10-year national mobilization" in the Green New Deal resolution has no start date. A mobilization is a large effort across the country. The 2021 and 2023 versions of the resolution used the same ten-year wording.
findings.use: The Green New Deal resolution sets no start date for its ten years. So anyone talking about it can say the ten years begin whenever they like.

a.q: as much as technologically feasible
as much as is technologically feasible

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution limits four emissions goals to what technology makes possible. No one is named to decide.
findings.plain: The Green New Deal resolution has goals for infrastructure, factories, farming and transportation. For each one, the goal is to remove emissions "as much as technologically feasible". That means as much as technology makes possible. The resolution does not say who gets to decide what is possible.
findings.tech: In a real law, a limit like "technologically feasible" gives power to whoever judges what is possible. That person decides how much must be done. The choice is usually based on facts from the industry that is being regulated. In the Green New Deal resolution, the phrase appears four times. It covers infrastructure, manufacturing, farming and transportation.
findings.use: Suppose a later law copied the Green New Deal phrase "technologically feasible". Then each industry's emissions goal would be only as strong as the choice about what is possible.

a.q: net-zero greenhouse gas emissions

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution calls for net-zero emissions with no deadline, starting point or way to count them.
findings.plain: The first goal of the Green New Deal resolution is net-zero greenhouse gas emissions. The resolution does not say by when. It does not say how emissions would be measured. It also does not say what counts as an offset, which is a step that makes up for emissions.
findings.tech: The Green New Deal resolution opens with "Whereas" paragraphs that give its reasons. They mention a need for net-zero emissions worldwide by 2050. The part that says what the House resolves ties the goals to a ten-year effort. But it sets no date for net-zero. The word "net" suggests that some emissions can be removed or made up for. The resolution does not say what counts.
findings.use: Supporters and critics can each describe the Green New Deal net-zero goal in their own way. Both can point to the resolution's words.

s.l: Coverage describing the goal as elimination within a decade

two.dec: Would a later law based on the Green New Deal resolution set a date to reach net-zero emissions?

views.why: Climate movement groups would want a deadline for the Green New Deal goal of net-zero emissions.

s.l: National Review

a.q: clean, renewable, and zero-emission energy sources

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution does not say which energy counts as clean, or if nuclear power does.
findings.plain: The Green New Deal resolution calls for all of the country's power to come from "clean, renewable, and zero-emission" sources. It does not say if a source must be all three or just one. That choice decides whether nuclear power counts.
findings.tech: Nuclear power plants give off no emissions, but they are not renewable. Renewable means the source does not run out. Fossil fuel plants that capture their carbon may be neither. Leaving the list open in the Green New Deal resolution may keep supporters with different views together. That is why this finding is treated as a trade-off.
findings.use: The Green New Deal resolution leaves the list of clean energy sources open. So a later bill that would actually become law would have to decide which sources count.

a.q: guaranteeing a job with a family-sustaining wage

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution talks about guaranteeing everyone a job. It creates no program, rules or money for it.
findings.plain: The Green New Deal resolution speaks of "guaranteeing a job" to all people in the United States. A real job guarantee needs a program, rules and money. It also needs an employer of last resort. That means an employer that hires people who cannot find other work. The resolution has none of these.
findings.tech: The same is true of other goals in the Green New Deal resolution. It calls for "guaranteeing universal access to clean water", which means clean water for all. It also calls for giving everyone "high-quality health care". In a measure that binds no one, these phrases only state goals.
findings.use: Someone can quote the word "guaranteeing" from the Green New Deal resolution. They can make it sound as if a job guarantee were already law.

findings.pat: One chamber cannot bind future legislation

a.q: ensuring that any infrastructure bill considered by Congress addresses climate change

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution says future infrastructure bills should deal with climate change. Its opinion does not bind them.
findings.plain: The Green New Deal resolution calls for any infrastructure bill in Congress to deal with climate change. Infrastructure means things like roads and bridges. But a statement of opinion by one chamber of Congress cannot control what later bills say.
findings.tech: The House and the Senate can each set official rules for their own work, and those rules do bind them. For example, a rule can let a member object to a bill that breaks it. A statement of opinion like the Green New Deal resolution is not one of those rules.

findings.title: The Green New Deal resolution gives no cost estimate. It provides no money for any of its goals.
findings.plain: The Green New Deal resolution sets goals that would take very large public spending. It gives no cost figure and sets aside no money. A statement of opinion could not set aside money anyway.
findings.tech: Only a bill or other measure that becomes law can approve or set aside federal money. The Green New Deal resolution mentions "adequate capital", meaning enough money. It says this could come through community grants, public banks and other public funding. But it gives no amounts.
findings.use: Supporters and opponents make claims about what the Green New Deal would cost. No one can check those claims against the resolution. It has no cost figures.

findings.pat: Vote taken on a different vehicle
findings.title: The House never voted on the Green New Deal resolution. A Senate vote on its text failed 0 to 57.
findings.plain: The House never voted on the Green New Deal resolution. The Senate majority leader, who leads the larger party there, brought the same text to the Senate. The Senate then voted on whether to take it up. That vote failed 0 to 57, and 43 senators voted present.
findings.tech: In the Senate, the same Green New Deal text was a joint resolution. That is a type of measure that can become law. Supporters of the House resolution called the vote a tactic and voted present. This shows how a measure that binds no one can be used to put members on record.
findings.use: Either side can use the Senate vote on the Green New Deal text. One side can call it proof of no support. The other side can call it proof of a sham process.

s.l: Senate roll call vote 52, 116th Congress
Coverage of the Senate vote

findings.title: Separate bills using the Green New Deal name would change the law if passed. The resolution itself would not.
findings.plain: Some people look for measures that would actually change the law. They should look at separate bills that use the Green New Deal name. Examples include bills on public housing and a Civilian Climate Corps.
findings.tech: Those Green New Deal bills are regular bills in the House and Senate. People would have to follow them if they became law. They can be checked for loopholes in the usual way.

s.l: Green New Deal for Public Housing Act reintroduction
2023 reintroduction with companion legislation

a.q: obtaining the free, prior, and informed consent of indigenous peoples for all decisions that affect indigenous peoples and their traditional territories

findings.title: The Green New Deal asks for indigenous consent to all decisions that affect them. Federal practice asks only for consultation.
findings.plain: The resolution says a Green New Deal will need indigenous peoples to agree to every decision that affects them or their lands. Today federal agencies only talk with tribes and ask for their views. In 2010 the United States backed a United Nations declaration on indigenous rights. It said consent means real talks, not always agreement. The resolution does not say which meaning it uses.
findings.tech: The resolution says a Green New Deal "will require" consent of indigenous peoples. That consent covers "all decisions that affect indigenous peoples and their traditional territories". A federal order says each agency must have a way to get "meaningful and timely input" from tribal officials. That order is about agency rules. In 2010 the State Department explained consent. It said consent calls for "a process of meaningful consultation with tribal leaders, but not necessarily the agreement of those leaders". The resolution uses the declaration's phrase. It does not accept or reject that reading. It applies the phrase to all decisions, not only agency rules. The resolution only states the House's view. So it changes neither the order nor the United States reading. The difference would matter for any binding bill that keeps the phrase.
findings.use: Supporters can cite the phrase as a promise of a consent standard. An agency could say the same phrase is met by the consultation it already does.

s.l: Executive Order 13175, Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments (2000)
U.S. Department of State, Announcement of U.S. Support for the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2010)

a.q: ensuring that frontline and vulnerable communities shall not be adversely affected

findings.title: The Green New Deal says frontline and vulnerable communities "shall not be adversely affected". It sets no limit on harm.
findings.plain: The resolution says frontline and vulnerable communities "shall not be adversely affected". It does not say how much harm is acceptable. It does not say how harm is weighed against benefits. This is the only place in the main text that uses "shall". The whole text is only the House's opinion, so the word does not make it binding.
findings.tech: The text reads "ensuring that frontline and vulnerable communities shall not be adversely affected". It is the only "shall" in the text. It sits under "it is the sense of the House of Representatives that", so it has no legal force. The standard has no limit. It sets no level of harm, no test of net benefit and no one to decide. The protected group is the full list in the definition of "frontline and vulnerable communities". Read literally, the standard would reach any project that harms even one member of those groups locally.
findings.use: If a binding bill kept this wording, people could cite it against nearly any project that has a local cost. A drafter would need to add a limit or a way to weigh harm.

a.q: (A) global reductions in greenhouse gas emissions from human sources of 40 to 60 percent from 2010 levels by 2030; and

findings.title: The Green New Deal gives carbon dioxide figures as if they covered all greenhouse gases.
findings.plain: The resolution has an opening part called the preamble. It says the world must cut greenhouse gas emissions 40 to 60 percent from 2010 levels by 2030. It also says the world must reach net-zero emissions by 2050. The report it cites comes from the IPCC, a United Nations climate science panel. That report gives those numbers for carbon dioxide only. Its central estimate is about 45 percent. For other gases such as methane, it describes deep cuts, not net zero by 2050.
findings.tech: The opening part of the resolution cites the IPCC Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5 °C. It asks for "global reductions in greenhouse gas emissions from human sources of 40 to 60 percent from 2010 levels by 2030". It also asks for "net-zero global emissions by 2050". The report says that in some paths "global net anthropogenic CO2 emissions decline by about 45% from 2010 levels by 2030". It gives a middle range of 40 to 60 percent. It also says "reaching net zero around 2050", with a middle range of 2045 to 2055. For other gases it says their cuts are "deep reductions". It gives methane and black carbon cuts of "35% or more of both by 2050 relative to 2010". So the resolution gives the carbon dioxide range as a range for all greenhouse gases. It also leaves out the 45 percent central estimate. This part has no legal effect, so it changes how the case is framed, not what the resolution does.
findings.use: Critics can point out that the figures do not match the cited report. Supporters can cite the same report for the carbon dioxide figures as it states them.

s.l: IPCC, Global Warming of 1.5 °C, Summary for Policymakers (2018)

a.q: (F) a risk of damage to $1,000,000,000,000 of public infrastructure and coastal real estate in the United States; and

findings.title: The Green New Deal ties $1 trillion of coastal risk to 2 degrees of warming. Its source calls it current.
findings.plain: The opening part of the resolution lists a risk to $1 trillion of public infrastructure and coastal real estate. It puts this among the effects of warming at or above 2 degrees Celsius. The Fourth National Climate Assessment, which it cites, says rising seas "now threaten" about $1 trillion in coastal real estate. That is a risk today. It is not tied to 2 degrees of warming.
findings.tech: The resolution blames its list of effects on "global warming at or above 2 degrees Celsius beyond preindustrialized levels". The Fourth National Climate Assessment says rising seas "now threaten approximately $1 trillion in national wealth held in coastal real estate". Its summary calls "America's trillion-dollar coastal property market and public infrastructure" threatened. Neither passage ties the figure to a warming level, a scenario or a date. The resolution gives a second figure. It is more than $500 billion in lost output each year by 2100. That figure was not found in the report text that was read. This finding does not cover it.
findings.use: People can fairly cite the figure as a risk today. Citing it as a result of 2 degrees of warming goes beyond what the source says.

s.l: Fourth National Climate Assessment, Volume II, Chapter 8: Coastal Effects

a.q: a large racial wealth divide amounting to a difference of 20 times more wealth between the average white family and the average black family

findings.title: The Green New Deal calls a 20 times wealth gap an average gap, but its source measured the median.
findings.plain: The opening part of the resolution says the average white family has 20 times more wealth than the average black family. The Pew Research Center study that reported a 20 times gap compared median wealth. Median wealth is the wealth of the household in the middle. The study used 2009 data. An average and a median can give very different ratios.
findings.tech: The resolution says there is "a difference of 20 times more wealth between the average white family and the average black family". It names no source for this. The Pew Research Center (July 26, 2011) said: "The median wealth of white households is 20 times that of black households". Pew used "newly available government data from 2009." So the ratio is a median ratio. The word "average" does not match it. The next item in the resolution uses "at the median" for the gender earnings gap. So the text treats the two terms as different elsewhere.
findings.use: A critic can call the wording inaccurate. The Pew figure supports the claim when it is stated as a median.

s.l: Pew Research Center, Wealth Gaps Rise to Record Highs Between Whites, Blacks, Hispanics (2011)

findings.pat: Named means narrower than the goal

a.q: removing greenhouse gases from the atmosphere and reducing pollution by restoring natural ecosystems through proven low-tech solutions that increase soil carbon storage, such as land preservation and afforestation

findings.title: The Green New Deal names only natural ways to remove greenhouse gases. Its climate report lists engineered ways too.
findings.plain: The net-zero goal depends on taking some greenhouse gases out of the air. The only ways the resolution names are natural ones, such as protecting land and planting forests. The IPCC report it cites says all of its 1.5 degree paths with little or no overshoot use carbon dioxide removal. It lists engineered methods next to forests. The resolution neither includes nor rules out those methods.
findings.tech: The resolution refers to "proven low-tech solutions that increase soil carbon storage, such as land preservation and afforestation". Another goal is about finding other sources of emissions and pollution. It is not about taking gas out of the air. The IPCC report looks at paths that keep warming to 1.5°C with limited or no overshoot. It says all of them "project the use of carbon dioxide removal (CDR)". It says this is on the order of 100 to 1000 GtCO2 over the 21st century. It says "Existing and potential CDR measures include afforestation and reforestation". It then lists engineered methods. These are bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), direct air carbon capture and storage, enhanced weathering and ocean alkalinization. The resolution has no rule on what counts toward "net". So the text leaves open the role of engineered removal.
findings.use: Some people favor engineered removal and some oppose it. Each side can say the resolution fits its view.

s.l: IPCC, Global Warming of 1.5 °C, Summary for Policymakers (2018)

a.q: more than $500,000,000,000 in lost annual economic output in the United States by the year 2100

findings.title: The Green New Deal ties $500 billion in yearly losses to 2 degrees of warming. Its source cites high emissions.
findings.plain: The resolution lists effects of warming at or above 2 degrees Celsius. One is more than $500 billion in lost yearly economic output by 2100. It cites the Fourth National Climate Assessment. That report says losses in some sectors could reach hundreds of billions of dollars a year by the end of the century. That is if warming goes on without big cuts in emissions. The plain review says losses this big come from high emissions, not from 2 degrees. The assessment pages read did not show the $500 billion figure.
findings.tech: The resolution blames some effects on "global warming at or above 2 degrees Celsius beyond preindustrialized levels". One effect is "more than $500,000,000,000 in lost annual economic output in the United States by the year 2100". The Volume II summary of the Fourth National Climate Assessment mentions "the continued warming that is projected to occur". That is warming "without significant reductions in global greenhouse gas emissions". It says losses in some sectors "could reach hundreds of billions of dollars per year by the end of this century." TechCrunch reported on the assessment. It quotes the assessment on "scenarios with high emissions and limited or no adaptation". There, "annual losses in some sectors are estimated" to grow to "hundreds of billions of dollars by the end of the century". TechCrunch sums up the total as "nearly half a trillion dollars annually by 2090". Chapter 29 gives sector figures, such as "$155 billion in lost wages per year by 2090". It gives no total across sectors on the page read. So the assessment links large losses to high emissions near the end of the century, not to a 2 degree line. The $500 billion number and its scenario were not found in the primary text. This point has not been checked against a source.
findings.use: Critics can say the resolution pairs a high-emissions figure with a 2 degree line. Supporters can quote the assessment's words on losses of hundreds of billions of dollars a year.

s.l: Fourth National Climate Assessment, Volume II, Summary Findings
Fourth National Climate Assessment, Volume II, Chapter 29: Reducing Risks Through Emissions Mitigation
TechCrunch on the Fourth National Climate Assessment, Volume II (2018)

a.q: the top 1 percent of earners accruing 91 percent of gains in the first few years of economic recovery after the Great Recession

findings.title: The Green New Deal says top earners got 91 percent of recovery gains. Its source later reports 52 percent.
findings.plain: The resolution says the top 1 percent of earners got 91 percent of income gains. That was in the first few years after the Great Recession. That matches economist Emmanuel Saez's estimate for 2009 to 2012. His later update covered 2009 to 2015. It found the top 1 percent got 52 percent of the gains over the first six years. The figure is right for the years it names. But the share fell as the recovery went on.
findings.tech: The resolution's clause on income inequality cites the top 1 percent. Saez updated his numbers with 2015 estimates. He wrote: "Hence, the top 1% captured 91% of the income gains in the first three years of the recovery." He also wrote: "Hence, the top 1% captured 52% of the income gains in the first six years of the recovery." The resolution says "the first few years". That fits the three-year figure. The plain review calls the figure later revised. The source shows instead that the longer period gives a lower share. The opening part of the resolution has no legal effect, as another finding in this review explains.
findings.use: Both sides can cite the same source. The three-year figure backs the resolution, and the six-year figure shows the share fell.

s.l: Emmanuel Saez, Striking it Richer: The Evolution of Top Incomes in the United States (updated with 2015 estimates)

a.q: life expectancy declining

findings.title: The Green New Deal says U.S. life expectancy is falling. That fit 2017 data, but 2018 data showed a rise.
findings.plain: The resolution lists falling life expectancy among current crises. It was introduced in February 2019. The latest final data then showed life expectancy falling to 78.6 years in 2017. The CDC later reported that it rose to 78.7 years in 2018. The statement was right when written, but the facts have changed.
findings.tech: The resolution's list of crises says "life expectancy declining". CDC Data Brief 328 says "Life expectancy for the U.S. population declined to 78.6 years in 2017". CDC Data Brief 355 says life expectancy "in 2018 was 78.7 years, an increase of 0.1 year from 2017." The resolution states a condition from one date as if it were current. Later versions would need current figures. The opening part of the resolution has no legal effect, as another finding in this review explains.
findings.use: Anyone quoting the resolution today should give the year of the data it reflects.

s.l: CDC National Center for Health Statistics, Data Brief No. 328, Mortality in the United States, 2017
CDC National Center for Health Statistics, Data Brief No. 355, Mortality in the United States, 2018

a.q: having emitted 20 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions through 2014

findings.title: The Green New Deal says the U.S. emitted 20 percent of global greenhouse gases through 2014. It names no source.
findings.plain: The resolution says the United States has emitted 20 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions through 2014. It does not say where the number comes from or what year the count starts. It does not say if the count covers only carbon dioxide or all gases and land use. Estimates of past responsibility differ with those choices. One widely reported study put the U.S. share of warming at about 20 percent from 1750 to 2005. It counted several gases and land use.
findings.tech: The resolution says "having emitted 20 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions through 2014". It gives no source, start year, list of gases or treatment of land use. Carbon Brief reported on a 2014 study. It says "The United States is responsible for a whopping 20 per cent of the warming". The study "examined each country's greenhouse gas emissions between 1750 and 2005". It counted "carbon dioxide from fossil fuel burning and land use change". It also counted "methane, nitrous oxide and sulphate aerosol emissions." That figure is a share of warming over a different period. It is not a share of emissions through 2014. So the resolution's exact measure could not be matched. The opening part of the resolution has no legal effect, as another finding in this review explains.
findings.use: Critics and supporters can each cite estimates that use different measures. The text gives no basis to choose among them.

s.l: Carbon Brief, UK tops list of world's biggest greenhouse gas emitters (2014)

a.q: the third-worst level of socioeconomic mobility in the developed world before the Great Recession

findings.title: The Green New Deal ranks the U.S. third-worst in mobility in the developed world. It names no study or countries.
findings.plain: The resolution says the United States had the third-worst socioeconomic mobility in the developed world. That was before the Great Recession. It names no source. Fact-checkers traced a similar claim to a 2010 OECD study. It ranked the United States 10th of 12 developed countries, which fits "third-worst". They also note that the exact rank depends on which countries are included.
findings.tech: PolitiFact (2013) looked at a similar claim. It says the research "did find the U.S. to be 10th among the 12 examined countries". It says "those 12 were all developed countries". It also says "America's exact ranking in those studies depends on which countries are surveyed." The study measured how much of a father's earnings edge passes to his son. That edge is "at least 40 percent of the economic advantage that high-earning fathers have over low-earning fathers". The plain review says the ranking also depends on the measure used. The source read speaks only to the choice of countries. The opening part of the resolution has no legal effect, as another finding in this review explains.
findings.use: The ranking can be cited with its source and sample. Without them, a critic can point to other samples with a different rank.

s.l: PolitiFact, Rep. Tim Ryan says United States ranks behind other countries in social mobility (2013)

findings.pat: Undefined limit on an existing power

a.q: eminent domain is not abused

findings.title: The Green New Deal says eminent domain must not be "abused" but does not define the word.
findings.plain: The resolution says a Green New Deal will require that eminent domain is not abused. Eminent domain is the power to take private land for public use. The resolution does not say what counts as abuse. It also calls for new power grid and rail projects over ten years. Federal law already lets some power line owners take land. These owners hold a federal permit. They may do so if they cannot reach a deal with the landowner. A binding version would have to say how the two fit together.
findings.tech: The resolution calls for "ensuring that public lands, waters, and oceans are protected and that eminent domain is not abused". It does not define "abused". It names no standard and no decision-maker. The Federal Power Act covers certain permits. It says "the permit holder may acquire the right-of-way by the exercise of the right of eminent domain". That applies when the holder cannot buy the land by contract or agree on pay. The Natural Gas Act gives a similar power to holders of pipeline certificates. It says "it may acquire the same by the exercise of the right of eminent domain". That happens "in the district court of the United States". The resolution calls for "energy-efficient, distributed, and \"smart\" power grids" and for "high-speed rail". It does not say if using these powers for Green New Deal projects would be allowed or would be abuse. It is a statement of opinion, so it changes neither law.
findings.use: Landowners and project opponents could read "not abused" as a limit on taking land for new lines. Developers could read it as fitting today's rules.

s.l: 16 U.S.C. 824p, Siting of interstate electric transmission facilities
15 U.S.C. 717f, Natural Gas Act certificates

findings.pat: Unstated input to a stated goal

a.q: to stop the transfer of jobs and pollution overseas

findings.title: The Green New Deal never mentions the minerals its clean power goals need, though other clauses affect their source.
findings.plain: The resolution calls for 100 percent clean power and zero-emission vehicle systems. It never mentions mining or minerals. The International Energy Agency says a typical electric car needs six times the mineral inputs of a conventional car. Mining at home could clash with the clauses on public lands and indigenous consent. Imports could clash with the goal of stopping the move of jobs and pollution overseas. The text does not say how to weigh these.
findings.tech: One goal is "meeting 100 percent of the power demand in the United States". It would use "clean, renewable, and zero-emission energy sources". Another goal is "zero-emission vehicle infrastructure and manufacturing". One limit is "to stop the transfer of jobs and pollution overseas". Another is protection of "public lands, waters, and oceans". A third is the consent of indigenous peoples. The words "mining" and "mineral" do not appear. The International Energy Agency (2021) says "A typical electric car requires six times the mineral inputs of a conventional car". It says "an onshore wind plant requires nine times more mineral resources" than "a similarly sized gas-fired power plant". It says energy-sector mineral needs "could increase by as much as six times by 2040" in climate-driven cases. Mining at home or imports might clash with those limits. That depends on project facts the text does not reach. The clash is stated here only as a possibility.
findings.use: Opponents can point to the missing supply plan. Supporters can argue the trade and land clauses set conditions on sourcing and do not forbid it.

s.l: International Energy Agency, Clean energy demand for critical minerals set to soar as the world pursues net zero goals (2021)

a.q: labor unions, worker cooperatives, civil society groups, academia, and businesses

findings.title: The Green New Deal names partners who may gain. It has no rules on conflicts of interest, audits or bidding.
findings.plain: The resolution says a Green New Deal must be built with groups such as unions, civil society groups and businesses. It also names worker co-ops, which are businesses owned by their workers. Several would also gain from other parts, such as the union-job goal and the capital and grants. The resolution has no rule that separates advising from getting paid. It has no rule on audits, inspectors general, competitive bidding or fraud. It is non-binding and spends nothing, so these gaps have no effect now. A law to carry it out would need to address them.
findings.tech: The resolution says a Green New Deal "must be developed through transparent and inclusive consultation". The partners include "labor unions" and "worker cooperatives", which means businesses owned by their workers. It also calls for "adequate capital". The money could come from "community grants, public banks, and other public financing". Other goals mention "high-quality union jobs". The only process value it states is "transparent and inclusive". No text covers conflicts of interest, audits, competitive awards or getting back misspent money. This review notes that no funds or duties exist to misuse. A binding version would have these gaps.
findings.use: Critics can cite the overlap between partners and people who get money. Drafters of binding bills can treat the list as the set of parties that need conflict rules.

findings.title: The Green New Deal combines climate goals with promises on jobs, health care, housing, education and trade.
findings.plain: Beside its climate goals, the resolution includes a job guarantee, high-quality health care and housing for all, and education that includes college. It also covers stronger labor rights, trade rules and freedom from monopolies. Each is a large policy area on its own. Because they share one text, a vote for or against it does not show a view on any one item. The climate parts cannot be weighed alone.
findings.tech: The goals outside climate include "high-quality education". It lists "a job with a family-sustaining wage" and "retirement security". It lists the right "to organize, unionize, and collectively bargain". It sets labor and wage standards "across all employers, industries, and sectors". It lists "trade rules" and "border adjustments". It lists freedom "from unfair competition". It lists "high-quality health care", "affordable" housing and "economic security". The resolution ties these to climate goals through "systemic injustices". The mix is a choice to build a wide group of backers around one plan. So it is labeled a trade-off. Another finding in this review covers the job guarantee alone.
findings.use: Supporters can present the whole agenda as one program. Opponents can cite any single item as a reason to oppose the whole.

a.q: creates high-quality union jobs that pay prevailing wages

findings.title: The Green New Deal calls for union jobs but does not say how that fits non-union contractors or right-to-work states.
findings.plain: The resolution says the mobilization should create high-quality union jobs that pay prevailing wages. It does not say if non-union contractors could do the work. Federal labor law lets states ban deals that make union membership a condition of a job. Right-to-work laws do this. The resolution does not say how its union-jobs goal would work in those states.
findings.tech: The resolution calls for "high-quality union jobs that pay prevailing wages". It also wants "wage and benefit parity". The National Labor Relations Act says "Nothing in this subchapter shall be construed as authorizing" some deals. These are deals "requiring membership in a labor organization as a condition of employment". That holds in a State where state law bans them. The resolution does not say what "union jobs" means. It could mean a union contract or union membership for each worker. It says nothing about non-union contractors. A binding bill could pursue the right "to organize" by amending federal law.
findings.use: Unions can read the goal as favoring union contractors. Non-union contractors and right-to-work states can read it as fitting open bidding.

s.l: 29 U.S.C. 164, National Labor Relations Act section 14

bigger.lead: The Green New Deal resolution names almost every part of the federal climate and economic agenda. But it is only a statement of opinion, so it changes none of them. The first table shows what the resolution names. The second table shows what a measure with the force of law would need for each goal.

map.note: The Green New Deal resolution makes net-zero emissions a goal. But it sets no limit, price or standard for emissions.
The Green New Deal resolution calls for power that is 100 percent clean, renewable and zero-emission. It does not say which sources count.
Some goals apply only as far as technology allows. These are the goals for infrastructure, industry, farming and transportation. The goal for upgrading buildings has no such limit.
The Green New Deal resolution does not say how much public money it would take or where that money would come from.
The Green New Deal resolution speaks of guarantees for jobs, wages and workers' rights. But it sets up no programs to deliver them.

map.part: Health care, housing and economic security
map.note: The Green New Deal resolution lists health care, housing and economic security. It says a Green New Deal will require them.
Later laws on clean energy spending and taxes were passed as separate bills. Sponsors of the 2023 version of the Green New Deal resolution pointed to those laws.

s.l: Sen. Wyden release on the 2023 reintroduction

map.note: The resolution has no rule on permits or environmental review. It only says eminent domain should not be abused. Eminent domain is the power to take private land for public use.
The text does not mention mining. It does not mention minerals either.
The resolution promotes sharing ideas and leading with other countries. It does not name the Paris Agreement.
The resolution calls for trade rules and border adjustments. It does not say how they would work.
The resolution asks for consent. Federal practice now asks only for consultation.

The resolution calls for building or upgrading grids and for affordable access to electricity. It does not mention keeping power steady during the shift. It does not mention delays in linking new projects to the grid.

map.part: Natural gas as a transition fuel
map.note: The resolution does not mention natural gas. One other finding in this review covers nuclear power and carbon capture.

map.part: Fossil-fuel revenue of states, tribes and localities
map.note: The resolution has no rule on the loss of fossil-fuel taxes or royalties. It does put investment first in communities that may struggle with the shift.
The resolution calls for resources, training and education. It does not say if enough trained workers exist for a ten-year timeline.
The resolution wants more clean energy equipment made at home. It does not mention solar panels and batteries from abroad.

map.part: Relocation of communities that cannot be protected in place
map.note: The resolution speaks of resiliency and climate risk. It does not mention moving communities.

The resolution's targets are global, and it aims to help other countries achieve a Green New Deal. The text does not explain how U.S. action connects to the global figures. EPA data show the United States produced about 15 percent of global emissions in 2014.

s.l: U.S. EPA, Global Greenhouse Gas Emissions Data (archived January 2021)

binding.need: A statutory target with dates and interim milestones; an agency with authority to set and enforce limits; a rule for what counts as an offset; a consequence if a milestone is missed.
A definition of qualifying sources; a standard that applies to utilities; a compliance schedule; penalties or alternative compliance payments.
A program and administering agency; eligibility and wage rules; an appropriation or mandatory funding stream.
Authorized programs with appropriations; standards; a delivery mechanism through States, localities or direct federal work.
Enforceable criteria for which communities qualify; a required share of investment; reporting and a right to challenge allocations.

stake.want: Labor unions want guaranteed jobs and wages. They also want protection for workers in industries that would shrink. Some unions backed the Green New Deal resolution.

stake.role: Fossil fuel companies and their workers
stake.want: Fossil fuel companies and their workers do not want a required end to fossil fuels. If one comes, they want it to take as long as possible.
Electric utilities want clear rules on which power sources will count, and time to build.
Supporters of nuclear energy want it to be clear that nuclear power counts as clean.

stake.role: Members of Congress focused on spending
stake.want: Members of Congress focused on spending want a cost figure first. They also want a source of money before any promise is made.

stake.role: Communities the resolution calls frontline and vulnerable
stake.want: Communities the Green New Deal resolution calls frontline and vulnerable want to come first when money is spent. They want a rule that can be enforced, not only a mention.
The sponsors of the Green New Deal resolution want it to set a direction. They want later bills to carry it out.
Opponents in Congress want a recorded vote that puts supporters on record. Opponents were the ones who set up the Senate vote on the Green New Deal text.

s.l: Senate roll call vote 52

stake.role: Nonpartisan analysts who work for Congress
stake.want: Nonpartisan analysts who work for Congress take no side. They say opinion statements like the Green New Deal resolution have no force of law.

s.l: CRS on sense-of resolutions

stake.role: A judge who reads laws by their exact words
stake.want: A judge who reads laws by their exact words applies those words as written. That judge will not fill in what Congress left out.

stake.role: A judge who reads laws by their purpose
stake.want: A judge who reads laws by their purpose settles doubts in favor of what the law was trying to do.
A person who drafts laws wants every key term defined. They want every reference checked. They also want every link to existing law clearly stated.

plain.conf_note: The Green New Deal resolution gives no job to any agency or official. So no one is in charge whose independence could be checked. A later law that carried out its goals would need this check.
